• Evidence of a causative link between ADHD and dietary surpluses of nutritional items such as sucrose or artiﬁcial food

• At group level, there is no conclusive evidence supporting dietary interventions for the treatment of ADHD.
• The few-foods diet allows the design of individually tailored diets and may offer treatment opportunities in subgroups of

• Further research is required to show the utility of nutrition-related interventions alone or in combination with other
treatment approaches in ADHD.
Introduction
While nutrition and diet are an established mainstay of physical and metabolic health, their role in mental health and disease is
less commonly recognized. However, considerable evidence points to an important role of nutrition in brain development and
functioning. Observational studies have consistently shown that the risk for mental disorders is associated with diet quality. A
range of macronutrients and micronutrients have been linked to behavioral, affective and cognitive functions as well as to the
incidence and prevalence of mental disorders. Nutritional deﬁciencies and other dietary factors have been suggested to be
involved in the etiology, pathophysiology, prevention, management, and modiﬁcation of common mental disorders, such as
depression, schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorder and attention-deﬁcit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Research on dietary
and nutritional approaches in the therapy of ADHD and other mental disorders has therefore attracted increasing scientiﬁc
interest.
The concept of ADHD has developed over the past 50 years, from its early description as a hyperkinetic reaction of childhood to
one of the most common diagnoses in child and adolescent psychiatry. ADHD is increasingly diagnosed in adults and is regarded as
